body.html: Viral diagnosis was once slow, costly and rarely useful, since few treatments existed. It is now routine because of the HIV epidemic and transplantation (many immunosuppressed patients at risk of opportunistic viruses), the growing number of antivirals whose use depends on a diagnosis, and technology such as monoclonal antibodies and PCR. There are three approaches: virus isolation, direct detection (antigen, particle or genome) and indirect detection (antibody response).

For the doctor, choosing the specimen is the most important step: the right specimen (e.g. nasopharyngeal swab, CSF, stool, vesicle fluid, blood on EDTA for PCR), taken at the right time (early, when viral shedding is highest), and stored and transported correctly: sent quickly in secure bags; if delayed overnight kept at 4 °C, not frozen, because freezing destroys enveloped viruses. The request form should give the date of onset, clinical signs and suspected diagnosis. Many errors are pre-analytical.

Historically in embryonated eggs (7-12-day chick embryos: chorioallantoic membrane, allantoic cavity, amniotic sac, yolk sac) and laboratory animals (mostly mice; costly and ethically limited). Cell culture, used since the 1960s, is the gold standard for isolation: the processed specimen is inoculated onto susceptible cells and observed for days or weeks for a cytopathic effect (CPE), then confirmed by antigen or genome detection. Sensitive and specific, and it yields the strain, but slow and demanding.

Electron microscopy identifies particles by size and shape (it discovered rotavirus, caliciviruses, astroviruses and HAV in stool) but needs 10⁵-10⁶ virions/mL; now mainly for research. Antigen detection gives results within hours and does not need live virus: immunofluorescence, immunoperoxidase, and enzyme immunoassays (rapid lateral-flow tests for SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV, rotavirus, norovirus; manual ELISA for circulating antigens such as HBsAg and HIV p24; automated chemiluminescence). It requires an accessible, stable antigen and a suitable (usually monoclonal) antibody.

Nucleic acid detection: extraction (organic, silica, magnetic beads), then PCR: denaturation (94-98 °C), annealing (50-60 °C), extension (72 °C) with a thermostable polymerase; RNA viruses need a reverse transcription step first. Labs are organised in one-way flow from clean to contaminated areas to avoid false positives. Real-time PCR measures fluorescence each cycle; the Ct value is inversely proportional to viral load and is used to monitor HIV, HBV and HCV treatment. Sequencing (Sanger or next-generation) detects drug resistance, determines genotype and tracks epidemics.

Indirect diagnosis shows the antibody response. IgM appears within 7-14 days and may persist for a month or more after clearance: it indicates recent infection. IgG appears after 10-14 days and may last for life: it indicates past infection or immunity, and a significant rise between paired sera (acute and convalescent) indicates recent infection. Most assays are immunoassays; point-of-care tests are increasingly used. A single positive IgG means very different things depending on the virus (e.g. immunity to rubella vs ongoing infection with HIV or HCV).

Acute gastroenteritis causes about 1.4 billion episodes and 2.2 million deaths a year, mostly in developing countries and in children. Causes include bacteria, parasites and above all viruses. The main viruses: rotavirus A, norovirus (GI, GII, GIV), sapovirus, enteric adenovirus 40/41 and astrovirus; rarer ones include Aichi virus, parechovirus, bocavirus and others. Transmission is faeco-oral: person to person (hands), contaminated food and water, surfaces, and sometimes aerosols (vomit). Detection: rapid antigen tests, ELISA and RT-qPCR.

The most common cause of acute diarrhoea in children under 5: about 200,000 deaths a year and 30-65% of hospitalisations for diarrhoea, with winter peaks. Family Reoviridae: naked, double-stranded RNA in 11 segments, so reassortment gives great diversity. Outer proteins VP7 (G types) and VP4 (P types) induce neutralising antibodies; VP6 is the group antigen. It is stable in the environment. Severity is scored with the Vesikari scale (20 points: 0-5 mild, 6-10 moderate, ≥11 severe); severity depends on age, not genotype.

The first cause of epidemic gastroenteritis at all ages (85-90% of viral outbreaks, about 267 million cases and 218,000 deaths a year), the second cause of sporadic diarrhoea in young children, and responsible for 31-87% of nosocomial diarrhoea. Family Caliciviridae: naked, (+)ssRNA, at least 7 genogroups; GII.4 dominates and changes every 2-3 years. In infants, rotavirus causes more moderate-to-severe disease, whereas norovirus causes more benign convulsions; premature babies can develop necrotising enterocolitis, apnoea or sepsis-like pictures.

No specific treatment: rehydration is the key. Standard precautions: hand hygiene, gloves, masks and eye protection for splashes, cleaning of equipment and surfaces, safe waste handling, patient isolation. Alcohol hand rubs are less effective against naked viruses such as norovirus; effective agents include bleach (chlorine), iodine products, peracetic acid, glutaraldehyde and ethanol ≥70%; quaternary ammoniums, chlorhexidine and ordinary soap solutions are not. Rotavirus vaccines: two oral vaccines (attenuated or reassortant) protect 90-96% against severe disease and greatly reduce hospitalisations, but do not prevent all infections; concerns include escape variants and lower efficacy in poor, malnourished populations. Norovirus vaccine: none yet (no easy culture system, high antigenic variability); mRNA candidates are in phase 3 trials.

Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, from viruses, drugs, toxins, alcohol or autoimmunity. It is acute if under 6 months and chronic if longer, when it can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Viral hepatitis causes about 1.4 million deaths a year (comparable to HIV or TB), almost all from HBV and HCV. Five viruses: A and E are enteric (faeco-oral, acute only, except HEV in the immunocompromised); B, C and D are blood-borne and can become chronic.

Picornaviridae (genus Hepatovirus), 27 nm, icosahedral, (+)ssRNA (7.5 kb); naked in faeces but 'quasi-enveloped' in blood. Spread faeco-orally (food, water, contacts). Incubation 14-28 days. Fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, dark urine, jaundice. Severity rises with age: children are mostly asymptomatic (<10% icteric), adults 70-80% icteric; mortality from 0.1% to about 2% after 40. Rare fulminant or cholestatic hepatitis; never chronic, no cirrhosis or cancer; recovery gives lifelong immunity. Diagnosis: anti-HAV IgM (positive for 8-12 weeks). IgM+ IgG+ = acute; IgM− IgG+ = past infection/immune; both − = not immune. Prevention: hygiene and an effective vaccine.

The slide's age table ends with '< 40 years'. It means over 40, where mortality is highest.

Hepeviridae, 27-34 nm, (+)ssRNA (7.2 kb), quasi-enveloped in blood. Mainly faeco-oral via contaminated water (large outbreaks in South and East Asia); also undercooked pork or game, transfusion and mother to child. Incubation 2-10 weeks (average 5-6). Usually acute and self-limiting, but can cause acute liver failure, notably in pregnant women; chronic infection occurs in the immunocompromised (e.g. transplant recipients). Extra-hepatic manifestations include neurological disorders. A recombinant vaccine (Hecolin) is licensed only in China.

Discovered as the 'Australia antigen' (1965-67). About 296 million chronic carriers worldwide and 820,000 deaths in 2019; prevalence in Morocco about 0.7%. Hepadnavirus: enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA replicating through reverse transcription; the envelope carries large, middle and small S proteins (HBsAg); several genotypes. Transmission: blood, sexual and mother to child. Outcome depends on age: in adults about 95% clear the infection (80% subclinical, 20% acute hepatitis, 0.1% fulminant) and ~5% become chronic; in infants 80-95% become chronic, with risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Markers: HBsAg (infection; > 6 months = chronic); anti-HBs (recovery or vaccination); anti-HBc IgM (acute); anti-HBc IgG (any past contact); HBeAg (active replication, high load); anti-HBe (low replication); HBV DNA (viral load, treatment monitoring). Test: donors, dialysis patients, pregnant women, babies of HBsAg+ mothers, household and sexual contacts, people with HIV, MSM, drug users, people from areas with prevalence ≥2%, patients before immunosuppression and anyone with unexplained raised ALT.

Treatment: nucleos(t)ide analogues (e.g. tenofovir) suppress the virus, reduce inflammation and fibrosis and lower (but do not eliminate) cancer risk; HBsAg loss is rare (max ~10% at 5 years). Cure definitions: sterilising (eradication, unlikely), functional (sustained HBsAg loss, the realistic goal), partial (HBsAg present, DNA undetectable). Vaccine: recombinant HBsAg, schedules 0-1-6 months or 0-1-2-12 months; also in combined hexavalent infant vaccines.

HDV is a defective (satellite) RNA virus that uses HBsAg as its envelope, so it only infects people with HBV. Incubation 30-150 days. Co-infection (HBV and HDV together): severe acute disease but low risk of chronicity. Superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier: usually chronic HDV with a high risk of severe liver disease. Diagnosis: anti-HDV antibodies, then HDV RNA in reference centres. HBV vaccination prevents HDV.

Discovered in 1989 (Nobel Prize 2020: Alter, Houghton, Rice). Flaviviridae (Hepacivirus), enveloped, (+)ssRNA (~9.6 kb), 7 genotypes. About 58 million chronic infections, 290,000 deaths in 2019; seroprevalence in Morocco about 0.5%. Mainly parenteral: transfusion before 1990, injecting drug use, transplants, unsafe medical procedures, tattooing, acupuncture, needlestick; perinatal about 6%; sexual transmission is rare. Most acute infections are silent and a majority become chronic, leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer. No vaccine.

Diagnosis: anti-HCV antibody (appears at least 4 weeks after infection, so not useful very early); if reactive, test HCV RNA: detected = current infection; not detected = past, resolved infection (or false-positive antibody). HCV core antigen can replace RNA. Treatment has gone from interferon (6-16% cure) to interferon plus ribavirin (40-55%) to direct-acting antivirals (since 2014, > 95% sustained virological response: no RNA 6 months after stopping). Hepatitis C is curable; WHO aims at elimination by 2030, which needs screening every adult at least once.

Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses (150-230 kb), 120-200 nm, with an icosahedral capsid and an envelope; replication is entirely nuclear (immediate-early activator proteins, early enzymes including DNA polymerase, rolling-circle DNA replication, late structural proteins, budding through the nuclear membrane). Their key property is latency: after primary infection they persist for life and can reactivate (stress, immunodeficiency, UV). Latent DNA is episomal (not integrated), with no replication or protein expression, so it escapes the immune system and antivirals. Latency sites: α (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV): sensory ganglia; β (CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7): blood, lymphoid tissue, glands, kidney; γ (EBV, HHV-8): lymphocytes. In healthy people infections are mostly benign; in the immunocompromised they cause severe infections and tumours.

These fragile viruses need close direct contact: saliva (HSV-1, CMV, EBV), respiratory route (VZV, outbreaks in groups), skin lesions (HSV, VZV), sex (HSV-2, CMV), mother to child (during pregnancy: CMV, VZV; at birth: HSV-2; after birth: HSV-1), and transfusion or transplantation (EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-8).

HSV-1 is acquired in childhood (70-95% of adults are seropositive) and causes oral, ocular and cerebral disease; HSV-2 is mainly sexually transmitted (genital herpes) and causes neonatal herpes. After oral infection latency is in the trigeminal ganglion, after genital infection in the sacral ganglia; recurrences are milder than the primary infection. Severe forms: herpes encephalitis (the first cause of viral encephalitis, acute necrotising and haemorrhagic, usually temporal; mortality over 70% untreated and heavy sequelae: a therapeutic emergency), keratitis (first infectious cause of blindness in industrialised countries), neonatal herpes (from maternal genital herpes during delivery; the mother is asymptomatic in two thirds of cases) and extensive herpes in the immunocompromised.

Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox on primary infection (a common childhood illness) and becomes latent in dorsal root (and cranial nerve) ganglia. Reactivation gives shingles (herpes zoster) in about 15%: a painful vesicular rash in one or adjacent dermatomes, more frequent with age and immunosuppression; ophthalmic zoster involves V1.

Epstein-Barr virus infects over 90% of people, spreads via saliva (kissing, shared cups and utensils), infects B cells and epithelium, and causes infectious mononucleosis (fatigue, fever, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly). It is oncogenic: Burkitt lymphoma (equatorial Africa), nasopharyngeal carcinoma (North Africa, Middle East, South Asia), Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas (especially in the immunocompromised), some gastric cancers.

Samples: fresh lesions, as early as possible, before antiseptics, transported fast in transport medium (fragile viruses); 1 day at +4 °C, −80 °C for culture, −20 °C for PCR. PCR is the diagnostic method. Treatment: aciclovir (nucleoside analogue) for HSV; aciclovir or mostly valaciclovir for VZV; foscarnet or cidofovir for aciclovir-resistant virus; ganciclovir, foscarnet or cidofovir for CMV. Prevention: the varicella vaccine (live attenuated, the first vaccine against a human herpesvirus; 2 doses from 12 months, at least 2 months apart; available as MMRV), the shingles vaccine from age 50 (Zostavax: live; Shingrix: recombinant subunit), and safer sex for HSV-2.

In 1850 Rigoni-Stern noticed that cervical cancer behaved like a sexually transmitted disease. HSV was suspected in 1965. In 1975-76 Meisels described koilocytes in precancerous lesions and Harald zur Hausen linked cervical cancer to papillomavirus (Nobel Prize 2008). Genotypes were split into high risk (cancer) and low risk (warts) around 1980, and in 1999 HPV DNA was found in 99.7% of cervical cancers.

Family Papillomaviridae (genus alpha-papillomavirus for the genital types): naked (non-enveloped), icosahedral, small (45-55 nm), with circular double-stranded DNA. There are more than 200 genotypes, classified by sequence, by tropism (cutaneous, mucosal, mixed) and by oncogenic potential: high-risk (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58...) and low-risk (6, 11: warts and condylomas). Transmission is by skin or mucosal contact, mainly sexual; mother-to-child transmission can cause recurrent laryngeal papillomatosis.

Cutaneous warts appear 1-3 months after inoculation (common warts on fingers, flat warts on the face, plantar warts); they can persist for years but eventually regress. Anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata): low-risk types 6 and 11. Cervical cancer: persistent high-risk infection progresses from CIN 1 (about half regress) to CIN 2/3 to invasive cancer over 7-30 years. HPV also causes anal, vulvar, penile and oropharyngeal cancers.

Cytology (Pap smear) looks for abnormal cervical cells; HPV DNA testing (PCR-based) detects high-risk types and is increasingly used as the primary screening test. The long preclinical phase lets screening find and treat high-grade lesions before cancer.

The most important preventive measure. The L1 capsid protein self-assembles into virus-like particles (VLPs), which contain no DNA and cannot infect. Bivalent (16, 18; Cervarix, 2007), quadrivalent (6, 11, 16, 18; Gardasil, 2006, girls and boys) and nonavalent (6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58; Gardasil 9, 2014). Given in 2 or 3 doses, ideally before sexual debut; WHO now also accepts a single dose in some schedules. Vaccination does not replace screening.

Smallpox is thought to have killed Pharaoh Ramses V (1196 BCE). 'Virus' is Latin for poisonous fluid. In the 1880s Pasteur (rabies) and Koch saw that some pathogens were invisible under the microscope. Ivanowski (1892) transmitted tobacco mosaic disease with extracts passed through a Chamberland filter: the agent was filterable. Beijerinck (1898) called it a 'contagium vivum fluidum' and showed it replicates in leaves. Landsteiner and Popper (1909) showed poliomyelitis was caused by a filterable agent, the first human viral disease recognised. Cell culture, electron microscopy, PCR and sequencing then opened the field.

Viruses are submicroscopic obligate intracellular parasites: they have no energy-generating system and no ribosomes, so they cannot make proteins alone (HIV has 9 genes and uses about 200 host dependency factors). Most are 12-400 nm, but size alone does not define them: Mimivirus (400 nm) is larger than the smallest bacteria (Mycoplasma, 200-300 nm). What makes them unique: virions are assembled from preformed components, they do not grow or divide, they contain only one type of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA), and they carry a receptor-binding protein to dock onto cells. Some bring their own enzymes (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase) but still need the host cell.

A virion is the complete particle: the genome (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid made of capsomeres (together the nucleocapsid), sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope taken from the host cell and carrying viral glycoproteins. The outer surface (capsid or envelope) binds the cellular receptor. The genome also encodes non-structural proteins: polymerases, reverse transcriptase, proteases and transcription factors.

By nucleic acid (DNA or RNA; single- or double-stranded; linear, circular or segmented), capsid symmetry (icosahedral, helical, complex such as poxviruses and bacteriophages) and envelope. Enveloped DNA viruses: herpesviruses, poxviruses, hepadnaviruses. Enveloped RNA viruses: flavi-, toga-, corona-, orthomyxo-, paramyxo-, rhabdo-, bunya-, filoviruses, HDV, and retroviruses. Naked DNA viruses: parvovirus, adenovirus, papillomavirus (papova). Naked RNA viruses: picornaviruses, HAV and HEV. By transmission: respiratory (influenza, rhinovirus, SARS-CoV-2), faeco-oral (HAV, polio, rotavirus), sexual (HIV, HBV), blood (HCV, HIV), zoonotic bites (rabies, arboviruses). The Baltimore system groups viruses by genome and replication: I dsDNA, II ssDNA, III dsRNA, IV (+)ssRNA, V (−)ssRNA, VI RNA with reverse transcription (retroviruses), VII DNA with reverse transcription (HBV). The official taxonomy is set by the ICTV.

Susceptibility: the cell has the receptor (defines tropism). Permissiveness: the cell supplies the factors for complete replication. Virulence usually reflects multiplication, but oncogenic viruses can cause lesions without it. The cycle has seven stages (about 6-8 hours): attachment, penetration, uncoating, genome replication, protein synthesis, assembly, release. Satellite viruses are defective and need a helper: hepatitis D needs HBV; adeno-associated virus needs adenovirus. Viroids are tiny circular RNAs that infect only plants.

RNA viruses mutate much faster (about 1 error per 10⁴-10⁵ nucleotides, roughly one mutation per genome per cycle) than DNA viruses (1 per 10⁸-10⁹), so they exist as quasispecies.

Emerging viruses are new diseases, mostly zoonoses with an animal reservoir; re-emerging ones are old diseases returning. Drivers: ecological and climate change, contact with reservoirs or vectors, travel and trade. Oncogenic viruses: HPV (cervical cancer), HBV and HCV (hepatocellular carcinoma), EBV (Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma), HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia). Control: antivirals (herpes, HIV, HCV), public health measures (hygiene, masks, condoms, quarantine) and vaccines: inactivated (polio, HAV, rabies), live attenuated (yellow fever), subunit (HBV), virus-like particles (HPV), reassortant (rotavirus, influenza), vectored (some SARS-CoV-2 vaccines).

'Myxo' refers to binding to mucoproteins on cells. Influenza viruses are enveloped, 100-200 nm, with single-stranded negative-sense RNA in 8 segments (about 13 kb) complexed with NP and the polymerase (PA, PB1, PB2) as helical ribonucleoproteins. The envelope carries about 500 spikes of haemagglutinin (HA) (attachment) and neuraminidase (NA) (release), plus the M2 ion channel. Types are defined by NP and M antigens: A (subtyped by HA 1-18 and NA 1-11; only H1, H2, H3 with N1 or N2 cause major human epidemics; origin in aquatic birds, infects many species), B (two lineages, Victoria and Yamagata, no subtypes), C (one HEF spike, mild). Avian H5 can infect humans but hardly spreads between people. Names follow: type / place / strain number / year (subtype), e.g. A/California/7/2009 (H1N1).

Antigenic drift: point mutations in HA (and NA) → annual epidemics. Antigenic shift: reassortment of segments between two viruses co-infecting one cell (e.g. avian and human strains in a pig) → a new subtype and a pandemic. 20th-century pandemics: 1918 Spanish flu (H1N1, over 50 million deaths), 1957 Asian (H2N2), 1968 Hong Kong (H3N2, still circulating), 1977 Russian (H1N1), 2009 swine flu (H1N1).

The virus infects ciliated respiratory epithelium, causing necrosis that favours bacterial superinfection; a strong cytokine response (IL-6, TNF-α) explains the systemic symptoms. Incubation is short (2-3 days); onset is sudden with fever 38-40 °C, chills, headache, myalgia, sometimes digestive signs, then cough and coryza. It usually resolves in a week; the epithelium regenerates in about 4 weeks. Pneumonia (viral or bacterial) causes most deaths; risk groups are infants, pregnant women, the obese, the elderly and immunocompromised. Diagnosis is clinical; lab tests (immunofluorescence on nasopharyngeal aspirate, rapid tests in 30 min, RT-qPCR) for severe or atypical cases, surveillance and hospital outbreaks.

Transmission: droplets (masks, distancing, ventilation) and fomites (hand hygiene, surface cleaning). Treatment: symptomatic, but no aspirin in children (Reye's syndrome); neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) within 48 hours for severe or at-risk patients; antibiotics only for proven bacterial complications. Vaccines: inactivated trivalent or quadrivalent (A/H1N1, A/H3N2, B lineages), updated yearly and given each autumn (egg allergy is the classic contraindication); a nasal live attenuated vaccine for ages 2-17. Priority: health workers, pregnant women, contacts of infants under 6 months, people with chronic disease, the elderly.

Enveloped, 150-200 nm, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (not segmented), helical nucleocapsid. They cause cell fusion and multinucleated giant cells (syncytia), spread by droplets and hands, and move rapidly through groups of children. Members: measles (morbillivirus), mumps (rubulavirus, parotitis), parainfluenza, and in the lecture's classification the pneumoviruses RSV and metapneumovirus.

The ICTV now places RSV and human metapneumovirus in a separate family, Pneumoviridae. Older slides and books still list them under Paramyxoviridae.

Extremely contagious, airborne, no animal reservoir. Incubation about 2 weeks to the rash. Prodrome of 2-3 days: fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, cough, and Koplik spots (white spots on a red base opposite the molars), pathognomonic. Then a maculopapular 'morbilliform' rash starting on the face and spreading to trunk and limbs over 2 days, fever up to 40 °C, bronchitis; it fades after 2-3 days. Complications: post-infectious encephalitis (~1/1000), giant cell pneumonia in the immunocompromised, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) years later (~1/1,000,000); secondary bacterial pneumonia and otitis. IgM, IgA and IgG appear with the rash; IgG lasts for life. Diagnosis is clinical; if needed, IgM serology, RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, giant cells. Management: supportive, vitamin A (2 doses 24 h apart); immunoglobulin within 3 days or vaccine within 72 h after exposure. Vaccine: live attenuated, usually as MMR, 2 doses (in the lecture's schedule 9 and 12 months).

RSV: highly contagious, winter epidemics, spread by aerosol and hands. Incubation about 5 days. In infants a cold can turn within 24 h into bronchiolitis (necrotising, with bronchiolar obstruction and patchy collapse) or pneumonia, with cyanosis and distress; dangerous at both extremes of age. Diagnosis: indirect immunofluorescence on nasopharyngeal cells (method of choice, immediate), ELISA, RT-qPCR; culture shows syncytia. Treatment is supportive; inhaled ribavirin only for high-risk infants; monoclonal antibodies protect high-risk babies. Prevention: vaccines for adults ≥60 and for pregnant women at 32-36 weeks, or a monoclonal antibody for infants under 8 months in their first season.

Parainfluenza 1-4: up to a third of respiratory infections, nearly half in young children. Types 1 and 2: laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), more in boys. Type 3: bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Diagnosis as for RSV.

Rabies is a zoonotic, progressive and fatal encephalitis caused by a Lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae). All warm-blooded animals can be infected. Pasteur showed its neurotropism (1881) and in 1885 vaccinated Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog. The virion is bullet-shaped (180 × 75 nm), enveloped, with non-segmented negative-sense RNA (order Mononegavirales) encoding five proteins: G (glycoprotein), N, M, NS (P) and L (polymerase). There are seven genotypes; genotype 1 is classical rabies worldwide.

Rabies affects more than 150 countries and kills tens of thousands of people a year, mostly in Asia and Africa. Dogs cause up to 99% of human cases; the urban cycle is maintained by stray dogs, the sylvatic cycle by wild carnivores (and pets in contact with them). In the Americas, where dog rabies has been nearly eliminated, bats now cause most human deaths. Children under 15 account for about 40% of bites. Some islands and countries are rabies-free thanks to quarantine or geography. WHO's goal (with a One Health approach) is zero human deaths from dog rabies by 2030.

Incubation is usually 2-3 months (from under a week to over a year), depending on the site of entry (closer to the brain = shorter) and viral load. The virus travels along peripheral nerves to the CNS. Early signs: fever and pain, tingling, itching or burning at the bite site. Furious rabies (most cases): hyperactivity, agitation, hydrophobia, aerophobia, hallucinations; death in a few days from cardiorespiratory arrest. Paralytic rabies (~20%): ascending paralysis from the bite site and slow coma; often misdiagnosed. Once symptoms appear, rabies is almost always fatal.

No test detects rabies before symptoms. Without hydrophobia or aerophobia, clinical diagnosis is hard. It is confirmed ante- or post-mortem by detecting virus, antigen or RNA in brain tissue, skin (nape biopsy) or saliva.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis for lab workers handling rabies virus, veterinarians, animal control staff and wildlife rangers. Post-exposure prophylaxis is an emergency: (1) wash the wound for at least 15 minutes with soap and water, detergent or povidone-iodine; (2) a course of WHO-standard vaccine (e.g. Verorab); (3) rabies immunoglobulin when indicated. Schedules used in Morocco for unvaccinated people: Essen (5 doses IM on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28) and Zagreb (2-1-1: two doses on day 0, then days 7 and 21). WHO categories: I (touch, lick on intact skin): wash only; II (nibble, minor scratch without bleeding): wash + vaccine; III (transdermal bite or scratch, saliva on mucosa or broken skin, bat contact): wash + vaccine + immunoglobulin.

Retroviruses are enveloped viruses with two copies of single-stranded positive-sense RNA and a reverse transcriptase that copies RNA into DNA, which is integrated into the host genome. Groups in the lecture: lentiviruses (HIV-1, HIV-2; also SIV, FIV: slow, persistent, fatal infections), oncoviruses (transforming: HTLV-1, the first human retrovirus isolated in 1980, causing adult T-cell leukaemia; HTLV-2) and spumaviruses (not pathogenic).

HIV was discovered in 1983 (Nobel Prize 2008: Barré-Sinoussi and Montagnier); the first AIDS cases were reported in June 1981. HIV-1 came from chimpanzee SIV (group M, which causes the global pandemic, probably crossed into humans in south-east Cameroon between 1884 and 1924; groups N and O are rare). HIV-2 came from sooty mangabey SIV, is found mainly in West Africa, and is less virulent and less transmissible. Virions are spherical, 90-120 nm. The genome (~9.2 kb) has 9 genes coding 15 proteins: gag (matrix, capsid p24, nucleocapsid), pol (protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase), env (gp120, gp41), regulatory genes (tat, rev) and accessory genes (vif, vpr, vpu/vpx, nef). HIV uses about 200 host dependency factors. Entry needs CD4 plus a co-receptor CCR5 or CXCR4.

Transmission: sexual, blood (shared needles: high risk; transfusion: now low risk with screening) and mother to child (pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding). HIV infects and destroys CD4 T cells. Primary infection: seroconversion within 15 days to 3 months; half have an acute illness (fever, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, rash, painful dysphagia, sometimes meningitis) with a mononucleosis-like blood picture and raised transaminases. Asymptomatic phase: clinically latent but biologically active, with continuous replication, lasting on average 8-10 years; persistent generalised lymphadenopathy in 20-50%. Minor symptomatic forms: candidiasis, shingles, warts, hairy leukoplakia, thrombocytopenia, and when CD4 < 200/mm³ fever, night sweats, weight loss > 10%, chronic diarrhoea. AIDS: opportunistic infections and tumours from profound immune depletion. Without treatment most die 10-15 years after infection; about 5% are long-term non-progressors and 5% rapid progressors.

Early diagnosis allows early treatment, better outcomes and less transmission; confidentiality is essential. Tests detect the virus (p24 antigen, HIV RNA by nucleic acid testing: early) or antibodies (ELISA, rapid tests, immunofluorescence, Western blot: from 2-3 weeks). Morocco uses a national algorithm for adults and children over 18 months; for exposed newborns, maternal antibodies cross the placenta, so PCR is needed. Monitoring: viral load (real-time PCR, HIV RNA/mL; two baseline measures, then every 3-6 months, and 4-6 weeks after starting or changing treatment) with CD4 count (flow cytometry).

Antiretroviral therapy (combination, usually triple) cannot eradicate HIV but stops replication; it is started early, whatever the stage, CD4 count or viral load, because it reduces illness, death and transmission. Adherence is essential. Prevention: condoms, needle exchange, screening of blood, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) and post-exposure prophylaxis. Morocco: first case 1986, low prevalence (~0.14%), most cases in Souss-Massa, Marrakech-Safi and Greater Casablanca, most affected age 25-44, and a large share of people unaware of their status; injecting drug use concentrated in the Oriental and Tangier-Tetouan regions.

HTLV-1 (5-10 million infected, probably more) causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) and HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP). It spreads through blood, breast milk and semen. Diagnosis: antibody immunoassay, confirmed by specific antibody tests or PCR. No vaccine and no treatment for asymptomatic carriers; care targets ATL and HAM/TSP. HTLV-2 usually causes no disease (possible neurological or chronic lung problems) and spreads by blood, sex, needles and from mother to child.

'Vaccine' comes from Latin vaccinus (of cows), after Jenner (1796) used cowpox from the hand of the milkmaid Sarah Nelms to protect against smallpox. A vaccine is a preparation of killed or attenuated organisms, or their products, that safely induces an immune response and prevents infection, reduces severity or hospitalisation. Viral epitopes induce both B-cell and T-cell immunity (neutralising antibodies and cytotoxic T cells), and memory can last years or a lifetime. Adjuvants boost the innate response. Milestones: smallpox and rabies vaccines, yellow fever grown in eggs, polio grown in cell culture, then protein, DNA and mRNA vaccines.

Live attenuated (no longer pathogenic but immunogenic): yellow fever, oral polio, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, rotavirus. Strong, long-lasting immunity but contraindicated in pregnancy and immunodeficiency. Inactivated whole virus: rabies, injectable (formalin-killed) polio, HAV. Split or subunit: 'split' influenza vaccine; recombinant protein: hepatitis B; virus-like particles: HPV. Viral vector (adenovirus) and nucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines, as for SARS-CoV-2: the cell makes the antigen (spike) itself. Most good viral vaccines protect over 90% of recipients.

Memory B cells need 3-4 days to raise antibodies above the protective level. That is enough for diseases with a long incubation (e.g. hepatitis B), but not for those with short incubation, which need antibodies to stay high (boosters). Herd immunity: when enough of the population is immune, transmission stops and the unvaccinated are protected too. Passive immunisation with human immunoglobulin gives immediate but temporary protection (about 4 months) after exposure to hepatitis A and B, measles, varicella, rabies; it can be given with inactivated vaccines (rabies, HBV). It works best before or soon after exposure and little once disease is advanced; in dengue, non-neutralising antibodies can worsen disease. Smallpox has been eradicated and polio almost; rhinoviruses and arboviruses (many serotypes) and HIV (constant antigenic change) remain without effective vaccines.

Viruses use the host cell's own machinery, so drugs that block them risk harming the cell: selectivity is difficult and toxicity a problem, unlike antibiotics that hit bacterial structures. About 50 antivirals are approved, for herpesviruses, CMV, HIV, influenza, HBV and HCV. Landmarks: idoxuridine and vidarabine (1962, toxic, limited); aciclovir (1983), proof that safe, highly effective antivirals are possible; interferon-α (1980s); zidovudine (AZT) (1990), the first useful HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitor; protease inhibitors and HAART (mid-1990s); lamivudine for HBV and neuraminidase inhibitors for influenza (early 2000s); direct-acting antivirals for HCV (from 2011). HCV cure shows what combination therapy can achieve.

Antivirals act at (1) entry (attachment, fusion), (2) nucleic acid synthesis (nucleoside analogues such as aciclovir, reverse transcriptase inhibitors, polymerase inhibitors), (3) late protein synthesis and processing (protease inhibitors), (4) assembly and (5) release (neuraminidase inhibitors). HIV is treated with combinations acting on several steps to prevent resistance.
